Maximum likelihood finds one set of weights, which gives one decision boundary. For two classes, such as stars and galaxies, this boundary is a straight line or hyperplane in the space of the photometric and morphological features. When two groups in the training data overlap little, many boundaries classify the training data almost equally well. A fit returns only one of them, and its predictions become more confident with distance from that boundary. An unusual object far from the training data can lie far from the boundary and receive a confident label that the data do not support. In astronomy, a confident error on such an object can hide a discovery.

The fitted model also gives a probability for each class. This probability tells us how uncertain the class of an object is for the fitted weights, for example near the boundary. It does not show how uncertain the weights are, because it is computed at one set of weights. The uncertainty of the weights is the topic of this chapter.

Two properties of astronomical data make the problem worse. Labeled data are scarce, because spectroscopic classifications and detailed morphologies need expensive telescope time and expert analysis. The labeled objects are also a biased sample, because astronomers tend to label objects that are easy to classify. Transitional and unusual objects are therefore poorly covered.

We want a classifier that reports lower confidence when the data cannot support a confident label. For an unusual object, its probability should then lie closer to 0.5 than the maximum likelihood probability. Bayesian logistic regression does this, and Figure 9.1 compares it with maximum likelihood for an unusual object.

Instead of finding a single decision boundary, we characterize our uncertainty about where the boundary should be placed. For this we use the posterior distribution of the weights given the data, as in Bayesian linear regression. In Chapter 5, the posterior \(p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D})\) given the data \(\mathcal{D}\) made predictions more uncertain far from the training data, and the same happens in classification. Boundaries sampled from the posterior, or from its Gaussian approximation below, show how much predictions vary in different regions of the feature space.

The likelihood contains the sigmoid of a linear combination of the features, so the posterior is not Gaussian. The sigmoid breaks the conjugacy of Bayesian linear regression (Chapter 5). There a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood gave a Gaussian posterior in closed form. Two approximations give a closed-form prediction. The Laplace approximation replaces the posterior by a Gaussian centered at its mode, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. The probit approximation then replaces the sigmoid by a function whose integral against a Gaussian has a closed form.

The result is a classifier that reports its confidence along with its prediction. In astronomical surveys, knowing when a model is uncertain can be as important as the classification itself.

9.1 The Bayesian Logistic Model

In this chapter we treat only binary classification, which simplifies the mathematics. The multi-class model of Chapter 8 can use the sampling methods of Chapters 12 and 13.

Binary logistic regression models the probability of class \(C_1\) for a feature vector \(\mathbf{x}\) with the sigmoid function. A constant 1 appended to \(\mathbf{x}\) makes the bias a component of the weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\). The probability is \[ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = y = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}}}. \] The probability of class \(C_0\) is \(1 - y\).

The likelihood of the labels is a product of Bernoulli probabilities \[ p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{X}) = \prod^N_{i=1} y_i^{t_i} (1 - y_i)^{(1-t_i)}. \] Here \(N\) is the number of data points and \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is the feature vector of data point \(i\). Its label \(t_i\) is 0 or 1 for the two classes, for example 0 for a star and 1 for a galaxy. The vector \(\mathbf{t}\) collects the labels and the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) the feature vectors, so we write \(\mathcal{D} = (\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X})\) for the data. The prediction \(y_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i)\) is the probability of class \(C_1\). Maximum likelihood finds the weights that maximize this likelihood, usually by minimizing the cross-entropy loss with gradient descent (Chapter 7).

The Bayesian Perspective

A finite data set is consistent with several decision boundaries. Some fit the training data slightly better than others, but many are plausible given the data. The Bayesian approach keeps these boundaries and gives each a probability given the data and the prior.

For example, suppose the training data contain two well-separated clusters. Many lines separate them without error. For such a line, larger weights make the sigmoid steeper and push each predicted probability closer to the correct label. The likelihood therefore keeps increasing, and no finite weights maximize it. A penalty on large weights or early stopping, both from Chapter 7, selects one boundary. The Bayesian approach instead averages over the plausible boundaries, and its prior keeps the weights finite.

Uncertainty about the weights becomes uncertainty about the predictions. To classify a new object, we compare the plausible boundaries. If they agree, we can be confident. If they disagree, the prediction is uncertain. Bayesian inference has three steps. We state a prior for the weights, update it with the observed data and use the resulting posterior distribution for predictions.

Prior and Posterior

We start with a prior that states our beliefs about the weights before we see the data. A common choice is a Gaussian prior \[ p(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{m}_0, \mathbf{S}_0). \] Here \(\mathbf{m}_0\) is the prior mean, our best guess of the weights. The matrix \(\mathbf{S}_0\) is the prior covariance, which describes our uncertainty.

This choice is mathematically convenient and often reasonable in practice. With no strong prior knowledge about which features matter, we can set \(\mathbf{m}_0 = \mathbf{0}\), which expresses no preference for any particular decision boundary orientation. The matrix \(\mathbf{S}_0\) then controls our confidence in this neutrality. Larger diagonal elements of \(\mathbf{S}_0\) mean greater prior uncertainty about the corresponding weights.

By Bayes’ theorem, the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood \[ p(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X}) \propto p(\mathbf{w}) \cdot p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{X}). \] Inserting the prior and the likelihood gives \[ p(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X}) \propto \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{m}_0, \mathbf{S}_0) \cdot \prod^N_{i=1} y_i^{t_i} (1 - y_i)^{(1-t_i)}. \]

Here we meet the first major challenge. The sigmoid makes the posterior non-Gaussian. This is the price of moving from regression, where outputs can be any real number, to classification, where outputs must lie between 0 and 1. The Gaussian prior is not conjugate to the sigmoid likelihood. We cannot write down a simple formula for it. We also cannot draw independent samples from it directly or compute predictions in closed form.

Why the Posterior Is Non-Gaussian

To see why, we compare the mathematical forms. The closed form of Chapter 5 depends on the exponent being quadratic in \(\mathbf{w}\). In Bayesian linear regression, the posterior was proportional to \[ p(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0)^T\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0)\right) \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})^T(\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})\right). \] Here \(\sigma^2\) is the noise variance of Chapter 5, and \(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix, called \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) in Chapter 5. Both factors are exponentials of quadratic forms in \(\mathbf{w}\), so their product is also the exponential of a quadratic form, which is another Gaussian.

In logistic regression, the posterior is proportional to \[ p(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0)^T\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0)\right) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)^{t_i}(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))^{1-t_i}. \] The first factor is still the exponential of a quadratic form. The second is a product of sigmoid functions. Its logarithm is a sum of terms with \(\ln\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)\) and \(\ln(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\), which are not quadratic in \(\mathbf{w}\), so the posterior is not Gaussian.

9.2 Intuition for the Laplace Approximation

Without a closed form, we approximate the posterior by a Gaussian, which is easier to handle. Near its peak, a smooth probability distribution looks like a Gaussian, and the Laplace approximation uses this fact. It becomes more accurate as the data set grows.

Consider the posterior \(p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{X})\) with a peak at \(\mathbf{w}_0\). If we zoom in on the peak, the logarithm of the distribution looks like a parabola.

A Gaussian is fixed by its mean and covariance. In the Laplace approximation, the mean is the mode of the posterior, the weights at which the posterior density is largest. The covariance follows from the curvature at the peak, which measures how quickly the density falls away from the mode.

The curvature is the negative second derivative of the log posterior with respect to the weights. A sharper peak has a larger curvature and gives a narrower Gaussian. Figure 9.2 shows the posterior of a model with one weight and the Gaussian from its mode and curvature.

The approximation works well under two conditions. The distribution has a single dominant mode, and most of its probability mass lies near that mode.

For Bayesian logistic regression with a Gaussian prior, both conditions are typically satisfied, especially as the data set grows. Well-separated clusters are the exception, as in the example of Section 9.1, because more data do not narrow the posterior along a separating direction. Along such a direction, larger weights give a better fit, so only the prior limits them.

Bernstein-von Mises Theorem

The Gaussian shape of the posterior for large data sets reflects the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. It states that posteriors tend toward Gaussian distributions as the sample size increases. This holds under mild conditions, for example a prior with non-zero density at the true parameter value. It also applies to posteriors of several parameters, as in logistic regression.

The Central Limit Theorem says that sums of many independent random variables approach a Gaussian distribution. The posterior behaves in a similar way, because the log likelihood is a sum with one term per data point. As the data set grows, this sum dominates the prior and narrows the posterior, so a second-order expansion around the mode becomes accurate. The Gaussian is centered at the maximum likelihood estimate, which approaches the true parameter value when the model is correct.

The Bernstein-von Mises theorem justifies the Laplace approximation for large data sets. Figure 9.3 shows the posterior of the one-weight model approaching a Gaussian as the number of data points grows.

In astronomical classification, a few observed objects allow many boundaries, so the posterior is spread out. With hundreds or thousands of labeled objects the plausible boundaries narrow. The Gaussian approximation is then good for classes that overlap slightly, and in surveys with thousands or millions of classified objects it is reliable. For small samples the posterior is skewed, as in panel (a) of Figure 9.3, and the Gaussian describes the uncertainty only roughly.

9.3 The Mathematics of the Laplace Approximation

We now derive the Laplace approximation, first for a single weight \(w\). Let \(p(w|\mathcal{D})\) be a non-Gaussian posterior distribution with one clear peak. In Bayesian inference we often know it only up to a normalization constant \[ p(w|\mathcal{D}) = \frac{f(w)}{Z}. \] Here \(f(w)\) is the unnormalized density and \(Z = \int f(w) \mathrm{d}w\) is the normalization constant. In Bayesian statistics this arises from Bayes’ theorem \[ p(w|\mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\mathcal{D}|w)p(w)}{p(\mathcal{D})}. \] The denominator \(p(\mathcal{D})\), the evidence, equals \(Z\) and is often hard or impossible to compute analytically. The Laplace approximation works directly with the unnormalized density \(f(w) = p(\mathcal{D}|w)p(w)\), the likelihood times the prior, and avoids this computation.

We approximate \(\ln f(w)\) near its peak by a quadratic function of \(w\). The logarithm of a Gaussian has this quadratic form, so exponentiating gives a Gaussian.

Derivation for One Weight

We first locate the mode \(w_0\), the point where the density reaches its maximum.

At the mode, the derivative of \(f(w)\) vanishes, and so does the derivative of \(\ln f(w)\) \[ \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}\ln f(w)\right|_{w=w_0} = 0. \] Working with the logarithm is often more convenient, as it transforms products into sums and simplifies our calculations.

We expand the log-density to second order in a Taylor series around the mode \[ \ln f(w) \approx \ln f(w_0) + \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}\ln f(w)\right|_{w=w_0}(w-w_0) + \frac{1}{2}\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}w^2}\ln f(w)\right|_{w=w_0}(w-w_0)^2. \]

The first derivative term vanishes because \(w_0\) is a maximum. The second derivative at a maximum is negative, which means downward curvature. We define the positive number \[ A = -\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}w^2}\ln f(w)\right|_{w=w_0}. \]The number \(A\) measures the sharpness of the peak. The quadratic approximation becomes \[ \ln f(w) \approx \ln f(w_0) - \frac{1}{2}A(w-w_0)^2. \]The quadratic approximation is the logarithm of a Gaussian with mean \(w_0\) and precision \(A\), the inverse variance.

Exponentiating the log-density approximation gives \[ f(w) \approx f(w_0)\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}A(w-w_0)^2\right). \]This is an unnormalized Gaussian. The constant factor \(f(w_0)\) sets the height and drops out when we normalize.

After normalization, we obtain the Gaussian approximation \(q(w)\) of the posterior \[ q(w) = \mathcal{N}(w|w_0, A^{-1}) = \sqrt{\frac{A}{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}A(w-w_0)^2\right). \]We find the mode \(w_0\), compute \(A\) from the second derivative of \(\ln f(w)\) there, and use the Gaussian with mean \(w_0\) and variance \(A^{-1}\).

Multivariate Extension

The weights of logistic regression form a vector, so we need several dimensions. The same steps apply, with vectors and matrices in place of scalars.

We find the mode \(\mathbf{w}_0\), where the gradient of the log density vanishes \[ \nabla \ln f(\mathbf{w})\Big|_{\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_0} = \mathbf{0}. \]

We then expand the log density to second order around the mode \[ \ln f(\mathbf{w}) \approx \ln f(\mathbf{w}_0) + (\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0)^T \nabla \ln f(\mathbf{w})\Big|_{\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_0} + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0)^T \nabla\nabla \ln f(\mathbf{w})\Big|_{\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_0} (\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0). \]The linear term vanishes at the mode, as in one dimension. The Hessian \(\mathbf{H}\) is the matrix of second derivatives of \(\ln f\) at the mode \[ \mathbf{H} = \nabla\nabla \ln f(\mathbf{w})\Big|_{\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_0}. \] Its elements are \(H_{jk} = \partial^2 \ln f/\partial w_j \partial w_k\) at \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}_0\). At a maximum, \(\mathbf{H}\) is negative definite, so the log density curves downward along each direction. Negative definite means that \(\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v} < 0\) for any nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\).

We define \(\mathbf{A} = -\mathbf{H}\), the negative Hessian, which is positive definite at a maximum, so its inverse exists. The approximation becomes \[ \ln f(\mathbf{w}) \approx \ln f(\mathbf{w}_0) - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0)^T \mathbf{A} (\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0). \]Exponentiating and normalizing gives the multivariate Gaussian approximation \[ q(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{\det(\mathbf{A})^{1/2}}{(2\pi)^{D/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0)^T \mathbf{A} (\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}_0)\right) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{w}_0, \mathbf{A}^{-1}), \] where \(\det(\mathbf{A})\) is the determinant of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(D\) is the dimension of \(\mathbf{w}\).

The factor \(\det(\mathbf{A})^{1/2}/(2\pi)^{D/2}\) makes the density integrate to one. A larger determinant \(\det(\mathbf{A})\) means a narrower Gaussian, so the factor grows to keep the integral at one.

9.4 The Laplace Approximation for Logistic Regression

We now apply the general result to logistic regression. This lets us quantify the uncertainty of the decision boundary, which matters for astronomical data that are sparse or unevenly sampled. Here \(f(\mathbf{w})\) is the unnormalized posterior \(p(\mathbf{w})\,p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X})\) of logistic regression, and the mode \(\mathbf{w}_0\) is the MAP estimate \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\).

Maximum likelihood maximizes the likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})\). The MAP estimate also uses the prior, because it maximizes the posterior \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w})\}. \]For a uniform prior, which treats all weight values alike, the MAP estimate equals the maximum likelihood estimate. For small data sets, an informative prior acts as a regularizer (Chapters 5 and 7).

The Laplace approximation needs the mode and the curvature of the log posterior, so we write the logarithm out first. Taking the logarithm of the product of the Gaussian prior and the Bernoulli likelihood of Section 9.1 gives \[\begin{aligned} \ln p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X}) &= \ln p(\mathbf{w}) + \ln p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X}) + \text{const} \\ &= -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0)^T\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0) \nonumber \\ &\quad + \sum_{i=1}^N [t_i\ln\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i) + (1-t_i)\ln(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))] + \text{const}. \end{aligned}\]In the second line, the first term comes from the prior. The second term is the familiar cross-entropy term of maximum likelihood estimation. The constants do not depend on \(\mathbf{w}\), so they do not move the mode.

Finding the MAP Estimate

The weights \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\) that maximize the log posterior make its gradient vanish. The gradient is the sum of the gradient of the log prior and the gradient of the log likelihood.

For the Gaussian prior, the gradient is \[\begin{aligned} \nabla \ln p(\mathbf{w}) &= -\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0). \end{aligned}\]

For the log likelihood, we use the gradient of the loss \(E\) from Chapter 7. The loss \(E\) is the negative log likelihood divided by \(N\). The gradient of the log likelihood is therefore minus \(N\) times the gradient of \(E\), so \[\begin{aligned} \nabla \ln p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X}) &= \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\mathbf{x}_i. \end{aligned}\] Each data point contributes its prediction error \(t_i - \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)\) times its feature vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\).

Combining the two terms and setting the gradient to zero gives \[ \nabla \ln p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X}) = -\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{m}_0) + \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{0}. \]The first term of this equation is the pull of the prior toward \(\mathbf{m}_0\). The second term is the pull of the data. At \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\) the two pulls cancel.

Unlike in linear regression, this equation has no closed-form solution. We find \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\) by gradient ascent \[ \mathbf{w}^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(\tau)} + \eta \nabla \ln p(\mathbf{w}^{(\tau)}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X}), \] where \(\eta\) is the learning rate and \(\tau\) counts the iterations, as in Chapter 7. The gradient here is a sum over \(N\) data points, while Chapter 7 uses their mean. For the same steps, \(\eta\) is therefore \(N\) times smaller than there. The sign is positive because we climb the log posterior to its maximum.

Computing the Hessian

Once gradient ascent has found \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\), we characterize the curvature of the log posterior there by computing its Hessian matrix. The Hessian of the log posterior is the sum of the Hessian of the log prior and the Hessian of the log likelihood.

For the Gaussian prior, the Hessian is \[\begin{aligned} \nabla\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{w}) &= -\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}. \end{aligned}\]

For the log likelihood, we differentiate its gradient again. The derivative of \(\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)\) with respect to \(\mathbf{w}\) is \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\mathbf{x}_i\), as in Chapter 7, so \[\begin{aligned} \nabla\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X}) &= -\sum_{i=1}^N \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T. \end{aligned}\]

The Laplace approximation needs the negative Hessian at \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\). It is the sum of the two contributions \[ \mathbf{A} = -\mathbf{H}|_{\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}} = \mathbf{S}_0^{-1} + \sum_{i=1}^N \sigma(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T\mathbf{x}_i)(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T. \]The matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the precision, the inverse covariance, of the Gaussian approximation to the posterior. The first term, the prior precision \(\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}\), describes our uncertainty before we see the data, and the second term adds the information from the observations.

The Final Approximation

With \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\), the Gaussian approximation of the posterior is \[ q(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}, \mathbf{A}^{-1}). \]This Gaussian describes the plausible decision boundaries, with the MAP boundary at the center. The covariance \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) describes the uncertainty of the weights. Larger diagonal elements of \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) mean greater uncertainty in the corresponding weights, and off-diagonal elements describe covariances between weights. A larger \(\mathbf{A}\) therefore means less uncertainty.

Points Near the Boundary

Write \(y_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T\mathbf{x}_i)\) for the prediction at the MAP weights. Each data point adds the term \(y_i(1-y_i)\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T\) to \(\mathbf{A}\). The factor \(y_i(1-y_i)\) has its maximum 0.25 on the decision boundary, where \(y_i = 0.5\) and the class probability is most uncertain. It falls toward 0 as a point moves away from the boundary. Points near the boundary therefore add the most to \(\mathbf{A}\), and they pin down the boundary best, because a small shift changes their classification. Points far from the boundary add little, because a small shift does not change their classification.

In Figure 9.4 the boundaries drawn from \(q(\mathbf{w})\) lie closer together after points near the boundary are added. Many points far from the boundary can still leave a large uncertainty about its position. A training set should therefore include points near the possible boundaries between classes, in addition to objects that cover the range of the features.

9.5 The Predictive Distribution

The Gaussian \(q(\mathbf{w})\) of the previous section is a distribution over decision boundaries. Each weight vector drawn from it gives a different boundary, and each boundary gives a different probability for a new object.

For a new object, one boundary might give a 70% probability of class 1 and another only 40%. This spread comes from our uncertainty about the boundary, and it is largest where the training data are sparse. We could examine the spread of these probabilities, but we usually want a single prediction that includes this uncertainty.

This leads us to the predictive distribution, the probability of a class label for a new input, as in Section 5.7 for regression. We consider all plausible boundaries simultaneously, and each contributes according to its posterior probability.

For a new input \(\mathbf{x}^*\) with unknown label \(t^*\), the predictive probability of class 1 is \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) = \int P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} | \mathcal{D}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}. \]The first factor \(P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{w})\) is the sigmoid \(\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^*)\), and the second factor \(p(\mathbf{w} | \mathcal{D})\) is the posterior of the weights. The integral is the average of the sigmoid over the weight vectors, each counted in proportion to its posterior density. Figure 9.5 shows boundaries sampled from the Gaussian approximation and the probabilities that they give for one object. The average of these probabilities estimates the predictive probability.

With the Gaussian approximation of the posterior, this becomes \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) \approx \int \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^*) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}, \mathbf{A}^{-1}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}. \]

Dimensional Reduction

The integral runs over the high-dimensional weight space, but the prediction needs only one number, the logit \(a = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^*\) (Chapter 7). The logit determines the class probability through the sigmoid. For a given weight vector, it is proportional to the signed distance of the point from the decision boundary. The distance is positive on the side of class 1 and negative on the other side.

Many weight vectors give the same logit \(a\) for a given input \(\mathbf{x}^*\). If we add a vector \(\mathbf{w}_{\perp}\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf{x}^*\) to the weight vector, the logit does not change \[ (\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{w}_{\perp})^T \mathbf{x}^* = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^* + \mathbf{w}_{\perp}^T \mathbf{x}^* = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^* = a, \] where \(\mathbf{w}_{\perp}^T \mathbf{x}^* = 0\) by definition.

The weight vectors with the same logit \(a\) therefore form a hyperplane perpendicular to \(\mathbf{x}^*\). The prediction is the same on this hyperplane, so only the distribution of the logit \(a\) matters. Under the Gaussian approximation, the weights are Gaussian. The logit \(a = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}^*\) is a linear combination of them, so it is also Gaussian, as for the regression line of Chapter 5.

The mean and variance of \(a\) follow from the rules for a linear transformation of a random vector (Chapter 3) \[\begin{aligned} \mu_a &= \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T\mathbf{x}^*, \\ \sigma_a^2 &= \mathbf{x}^{*T}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{x}^*. \end{aligned}\] Therefore \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_a, \sigma_a^2)\). The variance is large when \(\mathbf{x}^*\) points along directions in which the weights are poorly determined. Figure 9.6 shows this for two weights. The Gaussian over the weights in panel (a) gives the Gaussian distribution of \(a\) in panel (b).

The integral over \(\mathbf{w}\) therefore equals an integral over the distribution of \(a\). The predictive integral becomes \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) \approx \int \sigma(a) \mathcal{N}(a | \mu_a, \sigma_a^2) \mathrm{d}a. \]The mean \(\mu_a\) is our best estimate of the logit, and the variance \(\sigma_a^2\) is its uncertainty. This projection simplifies the problem. Weight vectors can have hundreds or thousands of components, so a direct integral over the weights is too expensive to compute. The integral over \(a\) has only one variable. The one-dimensional integral has no closed form, because the sigmoid does not combine with a Gaussian.

9.6 The Probit Approximation

To obtain a closed form, we replace the sigmoid by the probit function \(\Phi(x)\), the cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian distribution. The integral of this function against a Gaussian has a closed form.

The probit function is the integral of the standard Gaussian density \[ \Phi(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} \mathcal{N}(u | 0, 1) \mathrm{d}u. \]The value \(\Phi(x)\) is the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is at most \(x\). Figure 9.7 shows the density and the cumulative distribution function.

We can scale this function with a parameter \(\lambda > 0\), which gives \(\Phi(\lambda x)\), the integral of the standard Gaussian density up to \(\lambda x\). This scaling is equivalent to working with the random variable \(V = U/\lambda\) with \(U \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), which has the distribution \(V \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/\lambda^2)\), because \[ P(V < x) = P(U < \lambda x) = \Phi(\lambda x). \]

The probit function and the sigmoid both map the real line to the interval \((0,1)\) and increase along an S-shaped curve from 0 to 1. The two curves look similar, which suggests that one can approximate the other.

The Probit Identity

For \(\lambda > 0\), the integral of the probit function times a Gaussian is again a probit function \[ \int \Phi(\lambda a) \mathcal{N}(a | \mu, \sigma^2) \mathrm{d}a = \Phi\left(\frac{\lambda\mu}{\sqrt{1 + \lambda^2\sigma^2}}\right). \] Here \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the mean and variance of the Gaussian. For the predictive integral, \(\mu = \mu_a\) and \(\sigma^2 = \sigma_a^2\). Averaging a probit function over a Gaussian gives a probit function with a reduced argument, and the reduction grows with the variance.

We derive the identity with two independent random variables, \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/\lambda^2)\) and \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Here \(X\) is distributed like the scaled variable \(V\) above, and \(Y\) has the density \(\mathcal{N}(a|\mu,\sigma^2)\) of the integral. We calculate the probability \(P(X < Y)\) in two ways, which must give the same result.

First, we use the difference \(X - Y\). The two variables are independent and Gaussian, so the difference is Gaussian with mean \(\mathbb{E}[X-Y] = 0 - \mu = -\mu\) and variance \(\text{Var}[X-Y] = 1/\lambda^2 + \sigma^2\). Therefore \[ X - Y \sim \mathcal{N}(-\mu, 1/\lambda^2 + \sigma^2). \] The probability \(P(X < Y) = P(X - Y < 0)\) is \[\begin{aligned} P(X - Y < 0) &= \Phi\left(\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{1/\lambda^2 + \sigma^2}}\right) \\ &= \Phi\left(\frac{\lambda\mu}{\sqrt{1 + \lambda^2\sigma^2}}\right). \end{aligned}\]

Second, we condition on the value of \(Y\). For a value \(y\), the probability that \(X < y\) is \(\Phi(\lambda y)\). We weight it by the probability density of \(Y = y\) and integrate over \(y\). This gives \[ P(X < Y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \Phi(\lambda y) \mathcal{N}(y | \mu, \sigma^2) \mathrm{d}y. \]Both calculations give \(P(X < Y)\), so the two results are equal. This proves the identity, with the integration variable \(y\) in place of \(a\).

Sigmoid Approximation

To use the identity, we approximate the sigmoid by a scaled probit function \[ \sigma(a) \approx \Phi(\lambda a). \]

We fix \(\lambda\) by matching the slopes of the sigmoid and the probit function at \(a = 0\), the decision boundary, where the probability changes fastest. The derivative of the sigmoid is \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}a}\sigma(a) = \sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a)) = \frac{e^{-a}}{(1+e^{-a})^2}. \] At \(a = 0\) it equals \(1/4\). The derivative of the probit function is \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}a}\Phi(\lambda a) = \lambda\phi(\lambda a) = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\lambda^2a^2/2}, \] where \(\phi(x)\) is the density of the standard Gaussian. At \(a = 0\) it equals \(\lambda/\sqrt{2\pi}\). Equating the two slopes gives \[ \frac{1}{4} = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \implies \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}}. \]

With this value, both functions equal 0.5 at \(a = 0\) and have the same slope there. This gives a good local approximation at the decision boundary, where it matters most for classification. Figure 9.8 compares the two functions and shows the error for two other values of \(\lambda\).

The approximation is therefore \[ \sigma(a) \approx \Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}} a\right). \]Substituting \(\Phi(\sqrt{\pi/8}\,a)\) for \(\sigma(a)\) in the predictive integral and applying the identity with \(\lambda = \sqrt{\pi/8}\) gives \[ \int \Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}} a\right) \mathcal{N}(a | \mu_a, \sigma_a^2) \mathrm{d}a = \Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi/8} \cdot \mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + (\pi/8) \sigma_a^2}}\right). \]

To write the prediction in the form of standard logistic regression (Chapter 7), we use \(\Phi(\sqrt{\pi/8}\,x) \approx \sigma(x)\) with \(x = \mu_a/\sqrt{1 + \pi\sigma_a^2/8}\) \[ \Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi/8} \cdot \mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + (\pi/8) \sigma_a^2}}\right) \approx \sigma\left(\frac{\mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + \pi\sigma_a^2/8}}\right). \]The predictive probability is therefore \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) \approx \sigma\left(\frac{\mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + \pi\sigma_a^2/8}}\right). \]

The Uncertainty Factor

We define the uncertainty factor \(\kappa(\sigma_a^2) = (1 + \pi\sigma_a^2/8)^{-1/2}\) and write the prediction as \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) \approx \sigma(\kappa(\sigma_a^2) \cdot \mu_a). \]With \(\mu_a\) and \(\sigma_a^2\) written out, this is \[ P(t^* = 1 | \mathbf{x}^*, \mathcal{D}) \approx \sigma\left(\kappa(\mathbf{x}^{*T} \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{x}^*) \cdot \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T \mathbf{x}^*\right). \]The Bayesian prediction multiplies the logit \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T \mathbf{x}^*\) of standard logistic regression by \(\kappa(\sigma_a^2)\), which decreases as the variance \(\sigma_a^2\) of the logit grows. This is the behavior we asked for in the introduction, because the prediction is less confident where the training data constrain the weights poorly.

9.7 Properties of Bayesian Logistic Regression

We now ask where the variance \(\sigma_a^2\) is large and what it does to the prediction. The variance \(\sigma_a^2 = \mathbf{x}^{*T} \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{x}^*\) depends on the precision matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) of Section 9.4, which sums the prior precision and one term \(y_i(1-y_i)\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T\) for each training point. Since \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) is the covariance of the weights, \(\sigma_a^2\) is the uncertainty of the weights along the direction of \(\mathbf{x}^*\).

When \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is far from the training data, it has low similarity, as measured by inner products, with the training points \(\mathbf{x}_i\). The contributions to \(\mathbf{A}\) in the direction of \(\mathbf{x}^*\) are then small, so the corresponding elements of \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) are large. This gives a larger \(\sigma_a^2\) in regions far from the training data.

The minimum of \(\sigma_a^2\) lies near the center of the training points, weighted toward those close to the boundary, which add the most to \(\mathbf{A}\). The growth is fastest in the direction in which the training points near the boundary are least spread out. Weights along such a direction are poorly determined, so the variance rises quickly there.

Properties of the Uncertainty Factor

Standard logistic regression predicts \(\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T\mathbf{x}^*)\), which equals the maximum likelihood prediction for a flat prior. Three properties of \(\kappa\) show how the Bayesian prediction differs from it.

First, \(\kappa\) is positive and at most 1, because \(\sigma_a^2 \geq 0\) makes the factor under the square root at least 1. For \(\sigma_a^2 = 0\), which means no uncertainty about the logit, \(\kappa(0) = 1\) and the Bayesian prediction equals the standard one. As \(\sigma_a^2\) grows, \(\kappa\) decreases toward 0.

Second, a smaller \(\kappa(\sigma_a^2)\) moves the prediction closer to 0.5. Take \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}}^T \mathbf{x}^* = 2\), a strong positive prediction with \(\sigma(2) \approx 0.88\). For \(\kappa(\sigma_a^2) = 0.5\) we get \(\sigma(1) \approx 0.73\), and for \(\kappa(\sigma_a^2) = 0.2\) we get \(\sigma(0.4) \approx 0.60\). As \(\kappa\) approaches 0, the prediction approaches 0.5, the case of maximum uncertainty.

Third, for negative logits, which indicate class 0, the factor raises the prediction toward 0.5.

In a two-dimensional feature space with two overlapping clusters, standard logistic regression has a linear boundary. Its confidence increases with the distance from the boundary, even far from the training data.

In the Bayesian prediction, \(\sigma_a^2\) is small near the training points, where the predictions stay close to the standard ones. Away from them \(\sigma_a^2\) grows and the predictions move closer to 0.5. The 0.5 contour stays at the boundary of standard logistic regression. The other probability contours spread out, so the boundary becomes soft where evidence is scarce. Figure 9.9 compares the predictions of the two approaches.

Astronomical Applications

In astronomical classification, some objects lie outside the feature ranges of the training data. As an example, take the classification of galaxies as spiral or elliptical from morphological features. Suppose the training set contains mostly typical spiral and elliptical galaxies. Standard logistic regression can then give a peculiar galaxy a 99% probability, although nothing similar appears in the training data.

Bayesian logistic regression reduces this problem. For a galaxy unlike the training galaxies, the prediction lies closer to 0.5 than the standard one, and \(\sigma_a^2\) is large. Such a galaxy may be a new or transitional type.

First, objects with a large \(\sigma_a^2\) can be flagged for manual follow-up, while the other classifications can stay automatic. In large surveys, millions of objects can be classified automatically, and overconfident classifications can bias derived statistics or hide unusual objects.

Second, the variance helps to identify boundary cases that may be transitional or new object types. Many discoveries lie between established categories, for example galaxies in transformation, stars in unusual evolutionary states or entirely new classes. A large \(\sigma_a^2\) points to these cases.

A probability near 0.5 can also come from overlapping classes, and standard logistic regression already shows this. The variance \(\sigma_a^2\) adds the second cause, a poorly constrained boundary. These two causes are the aleatoric and the epistemic uncertainty of Chapter 5. The variance also shows where more labeled objects near the boundary would help most.

Other Sources of Uncertainty

Two more sources of uncertainty are not part of the model above. The first is the measurement error of the features of the object that we classify. We include it by averaging the probability over the true features \(\mathbf{x}\), given the measured features \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{obs}}\). The average is \(\int P(t^*=1|\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}_{\text{obs}})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}\), where the probability can be the maximum likelihood or the Bayesian one (Chapter 6 treats input errors for regression).

The second is error in the training data, in the labels and in the features. Some of these sources do not shrink as the training set grows. They include the overlap of the classes, the measurement errors of the new object and systematic errors in the training data. The uncertainty of the weights does shrink, as the Bernstein-von Mises theorem says. It therefore matters most for small or unrepresentative training sets and for objects far from the training data.

Bayesian logistic regression completes our treatment of linear models for regression and classification. In these models labeled data define a map from inputs to outputs, which is called supervised learning. Many astronomical data sets have no target variable to predict, such as galaxy measurements without known groups or survey spectra without known classes. In Chapter 10, we turn to such unsupervised problems, which look for structure in the data without labels. We start with principal component analysis, which finds the main directions of variation in high-dimensional data.

9.8 Tutorial: Uncertainty in Red Clump Classification

This tutorial adds an uncertainty to the red clump probabilities of Section 7.10 with the posterior and predictive distribution of this chapter. A survey must know how far to trust its probabilities, because the distance of a red giant branch star kept by mistake is less accurate. The full tutorial can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as tutorial 9.

The probabilities of Section 7.10 come from one set of weights, so they do not say how far to trust them. Other plausible boundaries fit the training stars almost as well and give a star next to the boundary a different probability. The Bayesian treatment thus keeps these boundaries and weighs each by its posterior probability (Section 9.1).

The sigmoid makes the posterior non-Gaussian, so the Laplace approximation replaces it with a Gaussian around the maximum a posteriori weights (Section 9.2). Weights drawn from this Gaussian give the plausible boundaries, and the predictive distribution averages the probabilities they give each star (Section 9.5).

Maximum likelihood gives one boundary (Figure 9.10a) and so one probability for each star. The Bayesian treatment gives the average of the plausible probabilities with their 95 percent interval, whose width shows how far to trust it. The width is largest at the dashed boundary, where the sigmoid is steepest, and almost zero far from it (Figure 9.10b).

The probability from one boundary and its interval answer different questions. The probability shows the overlap of the classes, an aleatoric uncertainty that more training stars do not remove. The interval measures our limited knowledge of the boundary, an epistemic uncertainty that shrinks as training stars are added. A survey that keeps stars above a cut can flag those whose interval reaches below it, because their classification is uncertain.

Further Reading

Zellner and Rossi (1984) gave a Bayesian analysis of binary response models. Albert and Chib (1993) developed latent-variable methods for binary and multi-class response models. Tierney and Kadane (1986) developed Laplace approximations for posterior moments and marginal densities. Walker (1969) examined posterior distributions for large samples, and Le Cam (1986) gave results, including the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. MacKay (2003) shows how to select hyperparameters in Bayesian logistic regression with the evidence. Bishop (2006) treats the Laplace approximation and the predictive distribution (Sections 4.4 and 4.5). McCullagh and Nelder (1989) treat generalized linear models. Kass and Raftery (1995) review Bayes factors and marginal likelihoods.
